title: What is Pediatric Basic Life Support?
objective: Define the pediatric basic life support
scenario: A healthy child was playing. The child suddenly collapses in a playground. Nearby people are confused. A nurse approaches.
prompt: What is Pediatric Basic Life Support (PBLS)?
fallbackText: A healthy child playing in a playground suddenly collapses. Bystanders look on, unsure what to do. A nurse approaches.

options.text: Emergency care provided to infants and children experiencing respiratory or cardiac arrest
Management provided during or while a baby was not crying after birth

feedback.text: PBLS is the emergency care given to infants and children in respiratory or cardiac arrest, until advanced help arrives.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Who needs Pediatric Basic Life Support?
objective: Enlist the conditions which require pediatric basic life support
scenario: The animation shows four children separately: one playing normally, one sleeping, one having an epileptic attack, and one who has become unresponsive.
prompt: Which child needs Pediatric Basic Life Support?
fallbackText: Four children are shown: one playing normally, one sleeping, one having a seizure, and one unresponsive.

options.text: The child having an epileptic attack

feedback.text: Unresponsiveness is the trigger for PBLS. Sleep, normal play and an ongoing seizure with breathing intact do not call for life support.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Why is PBLS important?
scenario: A heart and brain animation shows what happens to circulation and oxygen delivery when the heart stops.
prompt: Why is PBLS important?
fallbackText: An animation of the heart and brain shows oxygen delivery falling once circulation stops.

options.text: It helps maintain circulation and oxygen delivery until advanced care arrives

feedback.text: PBLS buys time. It sustains circulation and oxygen delivery to the brain and heart until advanced care can take over.

authoringNote: Source lists the type as Heart-Brain Animation; mapped to animation_mcq. Feedback text written for the build.

title: Emergencies requiring PBLS
objective: Enlist the conditions which require pediatric basic life support
prompt: Drag each condition into the correct box.

feedback.text: Drowning, choking, cardiac arrest and severe trauma can all progress to arrest. A cold or a mild fever does not call for life support.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Pediatric age group
objective: Identify the age group that comes under PBLS
prompt: Which age group is covered under Pediatric Basic Life Support?

options.text: Infants and children from birth until puberty

feedback.text: PBLS covers infants and children from birth until the onset of puberty. Beyond puberty, adult BLS applies.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Components of PBLS
objective: Define the pediatric basic life support
prompt: Which are the major components of PBLS?
fallbackText: An animation walks through the sequence of airway, breathing and circulation.

feedback.text: PBLS is built on airway, breathing and circulation. In cardiac arrest the order is CAB, with compressions started first.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Major cause of pediatric cardiac arrest
objective: Enumerate the causative factors that lead to pediatric cardiac arrest
prompt: What is the most common cause of pediatric cardiac arrest?

feedback.text: Unlike adults, pediatric cardiac arrest is usually secondary to respiratory compromise.

authoringNote: Source attaches a feedback video titled Physiology of the Pediatric Cardiac Arrest. Add the url to feedback.videoUrl once filmed.

title: Choking scenario
objective: Determine the physiology behind pediatric cardiac arrest
scenario: A 2-year-old child chokes on food and becomes unconscious.
prompt: What is the most likely mechanism leading to cardiac arrest?

feedback.text: Airway obstruction leads to hypoxia, progressing to cardiac arrest if untreated.

title: Adult versus pediatric cardiac arrest
objective: Differentiate between child and adult life support
prompt: What is the major difference between adult and pediatric cardiac arrest?

options.text: Pediatric arrest is usually caused by respiratory failure; adult arrest is often cardiac in origin

feedback.text: Understanding the underlying cause guides appropriate management.

title: NRP versus PBLS
objective: Determine the difference between NRP and PBLS
scenario: A newborn is not crying after birth. Separately, a 4-year-old is choking and unresponsive.
prompt: Which resuscitation approach is appropriate?

options.text: NRP for the newborn; PBLS for the 4-year-old

feedback.text: NRP is used for newborns, while PBLS is used for infants and children after the neonatal period.

title: Scene safety
scenario: A 4-year-old child is lying near an overturned electric heater.
prompt: What should you check first?
fallbackText: A child lies motionless on the floor beside an overturned electric heater that is still plugged in.

options.text: Check the scene and identify or remove hazards

feedback.text: Nothing else begins until the scene is safe. An electrical hazard must be removed before you approach the child.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Importance of scene safety
prompt: Why is verifying scene safety important?

options.text: To avoid becoming another victim while attempting rescue
To determine the cause of collapse

feedback.text: A rescuer who becomes a second casualty helps nobody. Your own safety comes before the child's.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Assessing responsiveness
scenario: The child is lying motionless.
prompt: How should responsiveness be assessed?

options.text: Tap the shoulder and shout loudly

feedback.text: Tap and shout. Vigorous shaking risks worsening an unseen spinal injury.

scenario: The child remains unresponsive.
prompt: What is your next action?

options.text: Activate the emergency response system and call for help

feedback.text: Help is summoned as early as possible, so that advanced care and a defibrillator are already on the way while you work.

title: Breathing assessment
prompt: Which breathing pattern suggests cardiac arrest?

feedback.text: Gasping is not breathing. Agonal gasps and absent breathing both point to cardiac arrest.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Pulse assessment time
prompt: What is the maximum pulse assessment time?

feedback.text: Spend no more than 10 seconds. If you are not certain a pulse is present within that time, begin compressions.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Infant pulse check
scenario: A 6-month-old infant.
prompt: Which is the correct pulse site?

feedback.text: The brachial pulse is used in infants. A short neck makes the carotid difficult to locate reliably.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Child pulse check
scenario: A 6-year-old child.
prompt: Which is the correct pulse site?

feedback.text: Carotid or femoral pulse is recommended.

title: Recognition of cardiac arrest
scenario: A 5-year-old drowning victim.
prompt: Drag each finding into the correct box.

feedback.text: Cardiac arrest is recognized by unresponsiveness, absent or abnormal breathing and absent pulse.

title: Pediatric Chain of Survival
objective: Describe the Pediatric Chain of Survival
scenario: A child drowning; the animation introduces the six links.
prompt: Which is the FIRST link in the Pediatric Chain of Survival?
fallbackText: The six links of the Pediatric Chain of Survival are introduced in order: prevention and early recognition, high-quality CPR, rapid defibrillation, advanced life support, post-cardiac-arrest care, recovery.

feedback.text: Prevention and early recognition reduce the likelihood of cardiac arrest and improve survival.

title: Arrange the Pediatric Chain of Survival
objective: Describe the Pediatric Chain of Survival
prompt: Arrange the Pediatric Chain of Survival in the correct order.

feedback.text: Following the chain in sequence maximizes survival.

title: Start CPR
scenario: A 6-year-old child is unresponsive, not breathing normally and has no pulse.
prompt: What should you do next?
fallbackText: A 6-year-old lies unresponsive. There is no normal breathing and no pulse can be found within ten seconds.

feedback.text: Unresponsive, not breathing normally and no pulse means cardiac arrest. Compressions begin at once.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Rescue breathing
scenario: The child has a pulse but is not breathing.
prompt: What is the correct management?
fallbackText: A child has a palpable pulse but is making no respiratory effort.

options.text: Provide rescue breathing, one breath every 2 to 3 seconds, 20 to 30 breaths per minute

feedback.text: Provide rescue breathing instead of CPR.

title: Compression rate
scenario: Three rescuers demonstrate different compression rates.
prompt: What is the recommended compression rate?
fallbackText: Three rescuers compress at visibly different speeds: slow, moderate and very fast.

feedback.text: Maintain 100 to 120 compressions per minute.

title: Compression depth in a child
prompt: What is the recommended compression depth in a child?
fallbackText: A cross-section animation shows the chest compressing to different depths.

options.text: About one third of chest depth, roughly 5 cm

feedback.text: Compress to about one third of the chest depth, roughly 5 cm in a child.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: Complete chest recoil
prompt: Why is complete chest recoil important?

options.text: It improves venous return and cardiac output

feedback.text: The chest must return fully between compressions so the heart can refill. Leaning on the chest reduces cardiac output.

title: High-quality CPR sequence
scenario: A 4-year-old child is unresponsive, apneic and pulseless.
prompt: Which sequence is correct?
fallbackText: A rescuer approaches a 4-year-old who is unresponsive, not breathing and without a pulse.

options.text: CAB with a rate of 100 to 120 per minute and correct depth

feedback.text: Follow CAB with minimal interruptions.

title: Compare two rescuers
prompt: Who performs CPR correctly?

sides.label: Rescuer A
parameters: Depth one half of the chest
Pauses for 20 seconds after compressions to discuss the next step

sides.label: Rescuer B
parameters: Depth one third of the chest, with full recoil after each compression
Provides ventilation with rescue breaths after 30 compressions

fallbackText: Rescuer A compresses at 70 per minute to half the chest depth, leans on the chest and pauses 20 seconds. Rescuer B compresses at 100 to 120 per minute to one third depth with full recoil, without interruption, and gives breaths after 30 compressions.

feedback.text: Correct rate, depth, recoil, minimal interruptions.

title: Long interruptions during CPR
scenario: A rescuer pauses compressions for 20 to 30 seconds.
prompt: Why is this harmful?
fallbackText: A rescuer stops compressions and holds the pause for 20 to 30 seconds.

options.text: It reduces blood flow to the heart and brain

feedback.text: Interruptions reduce perfusion.

title: Appropriate ventilation
scenario: Rescuer A gives a breath over 1 second with visible chest rise. Rescuer B gives rapid, forceful breaths.
prompt: Who ventilates appropriately?
fallbackText: Rescuer A delivers a breath over one second and the chest rises visibly. Rescuer B delivers rapid, forceful breaths.

feedback.text: A breath is given over about one second, just enough for visible chest rise. Rapid forceful breaths cause gastric inflation and raise intrathoracic pressure.

fallbackText: Live feedback shows rate 110 per minute, depth 5 cm and complete recoil, while the rescuer pauses compressions every 15 seconds.

feedback.text: Avoid unnecessary interruptions.

title: AED arrives during CPR
objective: Identify when an AED should be used
scenario: A 7-year-old child collapses during a football game. Assessment reveals the child is unresponsive, not breathing normally and has no pulse. CPR has been initiated. A bystander arrives carrying an AED.
prompt: What should the rescuer do NEXT?

options.text: Continue CPR and ignore the AED
Apply the AED as soon as it becomes available

feedback.text: Defibrillation is time critical. Apply the AED as soon as it arrives, minimising any pause in compressions.

title: Establishing a team leader
objective: Demonstrate appropriate leadership behaviors during a pediatric cardiac arrest
scenario: A 5-year-old child is in cardiac arrest. Four nurses arrive. Everyone starts talking simultaneously. No one is directing the resuscitation.
prompt: What is the MOST important action?

feedback.text: An effective resuscitation team requires a clearly identified leader.

title: Responding to an instruction
objective: Apply closed-loop communication during pediatric CPR
scenario: The leader says, apply the AED. The nurse remains silent and does nothing.
prompt: Which communication style is BEST?
fallbackText: The team leader instructs a nurse to apply the AED. The nurse stays silent and does not move.

feedback.text: Closed-loop communication confirms that instructions are heard and understood.

title: Identify the communication pattern
objective: Apply closed-loop communication during pediatric CPR
scenario: The leader says, Sarah, switch compressors. Sarah replies, switching compressors. After changing positions Sarah says, compressor changed.
prompt: This is an example of:
fallbackText: The leader asks Sarah to switch compressors. Sarah confirms she is switching, and confirms again once the change is complete.

feedback.text: The instruction is acknowledged on receipt and confirmed on completion. That closed loop is what tells the leader the task is actually done.

authoringNote: Feedback text written for the build; not present in the source document.

title: The compressor is tiring
objective: Assign roles and responsibilities effectively within the resuscitation team
scenario: The compressor appears exhausted and compression depth is decreasing. The team leader notices.
prompt: What should the leader do?

feedback.text: Compression quality falls with fatigue long before the rescuer notices. Rotating the compressor keeps depth and rate where they should be.

title: Full resuscitation
objective: Identify the principles of effective team dynamics during pediatric resuscitation
scenario: The team is performing CPR. The leader says, Maria, apply AED. Maria replies, applying AED. The AED is applied and Maria says, AED ready. The leader says, everyone clear. A shock is delivered. The leader says, resume CPR.
prompt: Which team dynamic principles are demonstrated?
fallbackText: During CPR the leader names Maria and asks her to apply the AED. Maria acknowledges, applies it, and reports it ready. The leader calls everyone clear, a shock is delivered, and the leader directs the team to resume CPR.

options.text: Leadership, role assignment and closed-loop communication

feedback.text: The leader directs, names a specific person for a specific task, and receives confirmation at each step. All three principles are present together.
